verses.note: Hebrews calls Noah an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith (Hebrews 11:7), and Ezekiel names him with Daniel and Job as a model of righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14). His blamelessness is not sinlessness, as chapter 9 shows; it is wholehearted integrity before God.

Paul reads the verse as God counting a person righteous apart from works, since Abram was declared righteous before circumcision and before the law (Romans 4:3-11, Galatians 3:6). James cites it to show that such faith is proved in obedience (James 2:21-23). Protestants have usually read ‘credited’ as God reckoning a righteousness not one's own; Roman Catholic and Orthodox readers have stressed that God's reckoning also makes a person righteous. All agree that the verse puts God's promise and Abram's trust before any merit.

The verb tsadaq here is a courtroom word: to be in the right in a dispute. Judah declares Tamar in the right with respect to her claim on his family. Genesis thus uses ‘righteous’ for faithfulness to a relationship's obligations, a sense the rest of Scripture builds on.

Judah's question, "How can we justify ourselves?", has no answer from the guilty side. He stops defending himself and leaves the verdict to the one who has the power to judge, which is the posture Scripture later describes when it says no one is justified by self-defense before God (Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:19-20).

‘You will be clean before the LORD’ describes a status God gives, not a condition the people achieve. The New Testament's language of being declared righteous before God builds on this Old Testament picture of cleansing received by God's appointment.

In Deuteronomy, righteousness names the right standing of a redeemed people who live faithfully in the covenant. Christians read Paul in different ways against this background. Some, including many Lutheran and Reformed readers, see a standard of law-righteousness that only Christ fulfilled; others, including advocates of the ‘new perspective’ such as E. P. Sanders and N. T. Wright, stress that Israel's obedience was always a response within grace.

The Servant makes many righteous by bearing their iniquities. The verse joins the forensic sense of justification (declaring righteous) with its ground (the righteous one carries the guilt of others). Paul's teaching that through one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19), and that Jesus was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25), rests on this verse's logic.

Daniel appeals to God's righteousness to save a people who have none of their own. This use of ‘righteousness’ for God's faithful saving action lies behind much of the New Testament's language of the righteousness of God revealed in the gospel, a connection interpreters since the Reformation have debated in detail (see Romans 3:21-26).

Protestant interpreters have often read the verse as showing that only a righteousness given by God (imputed righteousness) can meet the standard, while Catholic and many recent interpreters stress that Matthew means a transformed life. Both sides agree that Jesus requires more than outward observance; they differ on how that righteousness comes to be and how it relates to Paul's teaching (Romans 3:21-26; Philippians 3:9).

The verse does not make forgiveness a wage earned by forgiving others; Luke grounds forgiveness in God's grace (7:42, 15:20). It shows instead that those who have received mercy and refuse to extend it reveal that they have not understood it (Matthew 18:23-35).

The older son counts his standing by years of service and commands kept, which is why his father's generosity to his brother feels like injustice to him. The parable does not deny his obedience; it shows that obedience reckoned as wages cannot share the father's joy. Paul's contrast between a gift and wages (Romans 4:4-5) names the same difference.

John's language here parallels Paul's ‘no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 8:1): the believer does not come into judgment. The verdict of the last day is spoken now to the one who hears and believes.

This verse announces the doctrine the letter explains. Interpreters differ on its center. The Reformation tradition reads God's righteousness as the right standing God gives the sinner by faith. The New Perspective, associated with James Dunn (Romans 1-8, 1988) and N. T. Wright (What Saint Paul Really Said, 1997), reads it chiefly as God's faithfulness to his covenant promises, by which he creates one family of Jews and Gentiles. Critics such as Stephen Westerholm (Perspectives Old and New on Paul, 2004), Mark Seifrid, and Charles Lee Irons (The Righteousness of God, 2015) have argued that the Hebrew and Greek righteousness words concern God's justice and right order rather than covenant faithfulness as such. Many hold that God's saving action and the gift it bestows belong together in the phrase.

Interpreters read this verse in three main ways. Some, such as Douglas Moo (1996), take it as the law's principle in theory, which chapter 3 shows no one meets. Others, including C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner (1998), see the Spirit-produced obedience of believers, which will be acknowledged at the judgment. Others, such as N. T. Wright, speak of a future justification that accords with the whole life lived, while present justification is by faith. Kent Yinger (Paul, Judaism, and Judgment According to Deeds, 1999) showed how widely Jewish writers held together salvation by God's mercy and judgment according to deeds. All agree that Paul does not contradict 3:20-28.
No one is declared righteous by doing the law, because the law's function is to expose sin, not to remove it. The verse shuts the door that 3:21 opens in another place.

God's saving righteousness has appeared in history, apart from the law as the means of attaining it, yet in continuity with the law's own witness. The phrase ‘righteousness of God’ carries the same debate as in 1:17, and verses 25-26 show it includes God's own justice.
Righteousness is given ‘to all who believe’ without distinction. The same God, the same gift, and the same means for Jew and Gentile make justification by faith the foundation of one people of God.

Justification is God's gift, entirely free, and it comes to people who have sinned without their first improving. The redundancy of ‘freely by his grace’ is deliberate: nothing in the recipient pays for it.

This is the heart of Paul's doctrine: God is just and the justifier. Anselm's Why God Became Man (about 1098) and the Reformers' teaching on satisfaction both set out from the problem this verse solves, that forgiveness must not make God unjust.

Justification comes by faith, without works of the law as its ground. Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox traditions all confess that justification is by grace; the Council of Trent (1547) rejected the formula ‘faith alone’ as it understood it, while the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) between the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church stated a shared understanding that justification is by grace alone through faith, not on the basis of merit.

If justification were by works, the one justified would have something to boast about before God. That God excludes all such boasting is, for Paul, evidence that justification is not by works. Even the greatest of the patriarchs stands before God with nothing to claim.

God reckons righteousness to the one who believes. Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox theology differ over how this reckoning relates to inward renewal, but all read the verse as God's gracious verdict received by faith, and Paul's argument makes it the pattern for Jew and Gentile alike.

God justifies the ungodly, not the godly. The verse rules out any view in which God first requires people to become righteous and then declares them so; the verdict comes to people who have nothing to offer. That is why Paul grounds it in the atonement.

Paul equates having righteousness credited with having sins forgiven and not counted. Justification includes forgiveness at its core, whatever else it includes, and it is received as a blessing pronounced, not a reward earned.
Justification is anchored in two historical events, the cross and the empty tomb. It rests on what God has done in Christ, which is why Paul can move at once to peace with God in 5:1.

Justification is a completed verdict with present results. The first result Paul names is peace with God: the objective end of estrangement, which is why the feelings of the believer do not determine whether it is real.

Righteousness is called a gift, received. Whatever the nuances of ‘the righteousness of God’, this verse shows it includes a status given to believers, a point on which traditions that differ elsewhere largely agree.

The many are constituted righteous through the obedience of one. Whether the verse describes a legal verdict, a real renewal, or both, it roots the believer's righteousness in Christ's obedience rather than in his own.

‘Righteousness’ here is the outcome of obedience, which has led some to see a moral sense (righteous living) and others a reference to final vindication at the judgment. Either way it is not the ground of acceptance; Paul has already made that ground Christ's obedience (5:19).

‘No condemnation’ is the verdict of justification stated in its negative form: the sentence against sin is not reduced but removed. Paul grounds it in union with Christ, not in the believer's progress, which is why it can be stated in the present tense even after the struggle of chapter 7.
Justification stands in the middle of the chain, between God's call and his glorifying. It is God's act, rooted in his eternal purpose and certain of its outcome.

Justification is God's verdict, and no accuser can overturn it. Paul roots it in Christ's death, resurrection, and present intercession, so that the believer's security rests on the whole work of Christ.

Righteousness comes by faith, not by pursuit. The Gentiles who received it were not seeking it; the gift came to them in the gospel. Paul uses the verses as a bridge back to the justification by faith of chapters 3-4.

The verse defines justification negatively and positively: not by works of the law, but through faith in (or the faithfulness of) Jesus Christ. Even Jews, who had the law, came to be justified the same way as Gentiles, which removes the ground for ranking believers. Luther's Commentary on Galatians (1535) made this verse the center of Reformation teaching; Catholic theology, especially since the Council of Trent (1547), agrees that justification is by grace and not earned, while differing on how inner renewal belongs to it.

Being justified in Christ means admitting that one stands before God on the same footing as the ‘sinners’ of the Gentiles. That is not Christ's fault; it is the truth about everyone, and justification by faith exposes it.

Abraham is the proof that righteousness is reckoned, not achieved. What God counted to him was not a work but trust in God's promise, and that pattern, set before the law existed, becomes the pattern for Jew and Gentile alike.

Justification is ‘before God’, in his court, and Scripture itself says that life comes by faith. Paul reads Habakkuk's word to the faithful in a crisis as the principle of the whole relationship between God and his people.
The goal of the law's custody was justification by faith. Even the period of the law pointed beyond itself to the righteousness that would be given in Christ.

Though Ephesians uses ‘saved’ rather than ‘justified’, verses 8 and 9 state the same principle Paul applies to justification in Romans 3:27-28 and 4:2-5: human works cannot be the ground of standing before God, and so boasting is excluded.

Many Protestant readers hear in this verse a rest from works done to secure standing before God, matching Paul's contrast between faith and works. Others note that Hebrews does not speak the language of justification and read the rest chiefly as the completion of the believer's labors in the age to come (Revelation 14:13). The two readings are compatible.
God's not remembering sins is a judicial act: he does not bring them into account. The promise anticipates the settled standing before God that Paul calls justification (Romans 4:7-8).

The accuser's work was legal: to charge God's people before God. His expulsion means that no charge against them can stand, which is Paul's argument in Romans 8:33-34. The verse pictures justification from the courtroom's side: the prosecutor has been thrown out.
